Attribution: Nieman Reports [media_lens] https://niemanreports.org/documentarian-errol-morris-documentary-director-elizabeth-holmes-you-can-see-everything-nathan-fielder-thin-blue-line-shoah/

For more than four decades, documentary filmmaker Errol Morris has been fascinated by the gap between what people say and what they believe. In films including “The Thin Blue Line,” which investigates a wrongful death-row conviction in a police officer’s murder, and “The Fog of War: Eleven Lessons from the Life of Robert S. McNamara,” Morris has examined questions of guilt, responsibility, and the stories people tell themselves and others. His approach to interviewing is distinctive, too: He developed a device used by many filmmakers today called the Interrotron — a combination of the words “‘interview” and “terror”’ — that allows an interviewer and their subject to look directly into each other's eyes, creating an unusually intimate exchange. His interest in how people present themselves — and what they may or may not understand about their own actions — has also shaped Morris' connection to Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of the failed blood-testing startup Theranos, who has been in prison since May 2023 following her conviction on multiple federal fraud charges.

Sarah Alvarez has spent much of her career rethinking how local journalism can serve the public. After working as a civil rights attorney, then as a reporter and producer at the NPR station Michigan Public, she founded Outlier Media in 2016. Alvarez said the Detroit-based nonprofit newsroom was designed to fill information and accountability gaps in communities that were often overlooked by traditional news organizations.. One of its signature innovations, TXT OUTLIER, is a text message service Alvarez created to connect Detroiters directly with journalists and provide practical information on issues affecting their lives, from utility bills to housing and foreclosures. Under Alvarez’s leadership, Outlier also expanded its Documenters program, an initiative that trains and pays residents to attend and report on public meetings to create a public record of local government decisions in places that don’t have press coverage. The initiative has engaged more than 700 Detroiters and since spread nationwide, creating new opportunities for civic participation and public accountability.

With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

### 澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178049
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178049

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

### 儿童手表“小天才圈”调查：点赞成每日功课，有商家可解除家长管控
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-15 14:23 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32177210
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32177210

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

### 《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

### 演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178536
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178536

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

Attribution: Human Rights Watch [rights_humanitarian] https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/11/27/free-education-is-key-to-ending-child-marriage

Click to expand Image A student poses for a portrait in the classroom of her school in Koidu, Kono district, Sierra Leone, on November 24, 2020. © 2020 AP Photo/Leo Correa On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects. Every year, 12 million girls are married before 18 – that’s one every three seconds. Free education is a powerful tool to help prevent it. UNICEF estimates that if all girls completed secondary education, it could cut child marriage by two-thirds. Yet school fees and indirect costs — uniforms, transport, books, examinations — force girls out of school and into early marriage. Free secondary education helps keep girls in school through adolescence, when the risk of child marriage is greatest. Evidence from 14 African countries shows that making lower secondary education free and compulsory raised girls’ educational attainment by 1.6 years. And prevention needs to start earlier.

On November 26, 2025, Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades engulfed seven residential high-rise buildings at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po. The authorities initiated an independent investigation and arrested three dozen people implicated in crimes. The Housing Minister resigned. But the authorities have also threatened and arbitrarily arrested those engaging in criticism and activism concerning the fire. “The Hong Kong government responded to the horrific Wang Fuk Court fire by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/helping-european-firms-achieve-continental-scale-quantifying-economic-gains-28th

Europe’s fragmented business landscape can make it difficult for firms to expand across borders and reach scale. This column examines the economic case for a 28th European enterprise regime: an optional EU-wide legal framework covering firm formation, financing, and insolvency. Model-based simulations suggest that a comprehensive regime could raise EU GDP by around 3.3% after ten years and 4.4% after twenty years, with the ten-year gain equivalent to almost 15% of the current EU-US hourly labour productivity gap. The results also highlight the importance of covering the full firm life cycle, including restructuring and insolvency.

With public debt high across Europe, how fiscal consolidations affect productivity is again a live question. This column studies spending-based consolidations in 139 euro area regions between 1999 and 2019, using a new utilisation-adjusted measure of total factor productivity. In regions more exposed to consolidation, output falls while measured productivity rises. The productivity gains arise almost entirely within sectors and coincide with a net decline in business establishments.

Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/multimedia/do-glp-1s-help-people-work-more

Ozempic and Wegovy contain the same molecule, semaglutide, and both come from Denmark. The Danish state treats patients with type 2 diabetes by prescribing Ozempic with a public subsidy. Someone who takes Wegovy to lose weight pays the full price, around €4,000 a year. Raül Santaeulàlia-Llopis (NYU Abu Dhabi, CEPR), Veda Narasimhan (NYU Abu Dhabi) and Fane Groes (Copenhagen Business School) followed both groups, to discover how taking the drug changed their work. Diabetic patients often had trouble working, so would they be more likely to hold a job after treatment began? The weight-loss group were more likely to have jobs already, but would they work longer hours? If more people are working for longer, can the income tax on those extra hours of work pay for that government subsidy?

European users account for roughly 38% of global stablecoin transaction volume – almost entirely in dollar-denominated tokens with shutdown mechanisms written into their software. This column argues that while Europe's regulatory response has been substantial, it is calibrated to a different threat. Europe should conduct audits not just of the money backing a token, but of the code that can freeze it. And the EU Blocking Statute should be modernised so it can operate on code-based restrictions, not only administrative orders.

The 2026 Nobel prize in economics was awarded to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for providing microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation policy. This column outlines the contributions of Michael Woodford, particularly to the development of the new Keynesian model. This model introduces nominal rigidities into a general equilibrium framework in which individual households and firms make decisions. In doing so, the model has had significant implications: it justifies monetary stabilisation policy using the nominal interest rate to control the price level, makes the case for inflation targeting, and provides the rationale for more transparent central bank communication and forward guidance.

Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/explaining-stock-market-why-it-still-so-hard

Physicists could already explain the motion of planets with extraordinary precision centuries ago. Finance still struggles to explain yesterday’s stock market movement. This column identifies a foundational failure of empirical asset pricing and makes significant progress towards explaining market movements using AI. Conventional measures account for remarkably little return variation, even with hindsight. Reasons extracted with AI from just one Wall Street Journal market recap per trading day explain about 30% of daily and 40% of monthly S&P 500 return variation out of sample.

### Designing Low Emission Zones: Theory and Evidence -- by Nano Barahona, Natalia Fabra, Imelda, Juan-Pablo Montero
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w36037#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w36037#fromrss

Low Emission Zones (LEZs), which exclude polluting vehicles from parts of a city, are spreading. Yet how their design affects welfare is poorly understood. Unlike price instruments, LEZs ration access inefficiently, imposing costs on inframarginal drivers of restricted vehicles. In our model, welfare is quasi-convex in LEZ size, yielding bang-bang principles: LEZs should be as large as possible or not implemented at all; cleaner vehicles (e.g., hybrids) could be exempt as transition technologies but later restricted, which may require planner commitment. Using new-car purchases, we find Madrid’s LEZ shifted buyers toward cleaner cars, but the surplus losses of switchers and inframarginal drivers exceeded emission savings.

### Five Facts About Stablecoins -- by Lin William Cong, Gordon Y. Liao, Eswar S. Prasad, Tony Zhang
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w36038#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w36038#fromrss

We document five facts about payment stablecoins using wallet-level blockchain data from 2020 to 2025. First, stablecoins serve as a transaction currency: onchain volume exceeds Bitcoin’s despite a much smaller supply, velocity has risen sharply, and transactions have shifted toward low-value transfers. Second, using transaction timing to refine exchange-based attribution, we find activity spread across the Americas, Europe, and Asia and fewer cross-regional flows than the standard method implies. Third, we estimate a structural cash-management model on the holdings data and find that the costs of accessing stablecoin wallets have fallen since 2023. Fourth, stablecoins are becoming the settlement currency of a fast-growing onchain credit market, and their growth appears to reallocate rather than destroy credit. Fifth, smart contracts are involved in about a third of Ethereum stablecoin transactions and over two thirds of volume, and protocols such as x402 demonstrate sub-cent machine-to-machine payments.

### Democratizing Venture Capital: Tax Incentives and the Geographic Expansion of Startup Investing -- by Murillo Campello, Guilherme Junqueira
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w36039#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w36039#fromrss

Can tax subsidies expand the geographic reach of startup investing? Despite decades of growth, venture capital (VC) remains concentrated in a handful of metropolitan areas, leaving most of the country with limited access to startup financing. We study the 2009–2010 enhancement of the Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) program, which eliminated federal capital gains taxes on investments in qualifying startups. By raising the payoff to success, the reform made riskier investments more attractive, including entry into unfamiliar markets. This incentive is especially strong for VC funds. Relative to similarly sized metros that already had VC, the reform raised the probability that a previously unserved metro received VC investment in qualifying sectors by 8 to 10 percentage points. There was no comparable increase in sectors excluded from QSBS or among angel investors, who receive the same tax benefit. Startups in newly served markets performed like those in other non-hub markets, created high-wage jobs, and attracted scientific and technical workers, some from established hubs.

Source: NBER

This article documents the integration of the American capital market with the first long-run, geolocated, firm-level record of the asset holdings of large institutional investors: over 100,000 holdings of life insurers, 1870–1940. Between 1880 and 1890 the mean distance of insurers’ bonds from home more than doubled and their home-state share fell from over half to under a quarter. The shift occurred within firms, across bond classes and charters. Mortgage lending was national wherever state law permitted it. Integration was largely complete by 1890.

### Does Treating Addiction Rebuild Lives? Evidence from Buprenorphine -- by Sarah Eichmeyer, Aljoscha Janssen, Jonathan Zhang
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w36041#fromrss

Does treating addiction improve economic circumstances as well as health? Using two decades of Veterans Health Administration records on over 140,000 patients with opioid use disorder and consumer credit data, we exploit staggered facility-level buprenorphine adoption and quasi-random emergency physician assignment. A five-percentage-point increase in the share of clinicians with buprenorphine prescribing experience doubles overdose survivors’ long-term medication use and reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 3.7 percentage points. Instrumenting receipt yields a 22 percent credit score gain. At $300,000 per statistical life-year, estimated survival benefits alone exceed added medical costs within three years

### The Effects of Private Plan Subsidies on Enrollment: Evidence from Medicare Advantage -- by Paul D. Jacobs, Timothy J. Layton
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w36042#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w36042#fromrss

Some social insurance programs, including the Medicare program in the United States, allow beneficiaries to choose between public and private insurance firms. In these types of programs, the government will often provide a voucher to those who opt for private firms. A key policy decision is the level of this voucher, and a key input to that decision is the elasticity of enrollment in the public versus the private option with respect to the size of the voucher. We estimate this elasticity in the Medicare program, where recent work has provided remarkably little evidence on how Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollment responds to payment despite the program’s rapid growth. We leverage the fact that the formula determining county-level “benchmark” payments (vouchers) involves coarse thresholds based on county-level spending and counties occasionally move across these thresholds, providing a shock to the vouchers unrelated to beneficiary demand.

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: LessWrong [public_ideas] https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/6w3Cxe7jb8yJ8CFm5/insufficiently-rat-resistant-trash-bins

Somerville has had a rat problem for a long time, and in June 2014 issued rodent-resistant trash bins: The new carts' sturdy construction and secure-fitting lids will keep out rodents, denying them a food source, and will result in fewer blown-over barrels, helping to keep streets clean and attractive on trash days. The plastic is tough, but our rats are tougher. They now rapidly chew holes through new bins: we got ours replaced (first one is free) and they chewed through within weeks. If you cover the holes with metal screen, they get through that too: We've resorted to keeping our trash in a traditional metal trash can, the kind you'd get for a Faraday cage. On the morning of trash day we'll move the bags over to the city bins. This has worked well for us, and while rats are adaptable I'm optimistic that, unlike plastic and window screen, solid steel is a material they will not figure out how to chew through. What I'd like even more, though, is a metal one the same shape as the city's.

In this post, I’ll share a summary of a recent research project, in which I investigate the existence and strength of moral concepts in models that are not language models. I provide evidence that some moral judgment capabilities exist and emerge even in a model that was never trained on them (and never saw any text modality at all!) Modern LLMs clearly have some sense of moral values (Schramowski et al., 2022), and can tell you a lot about what would be considered good and virtuous vs. what would be bad or evil behaviour. This is not surprising - the textual training corpus of these models includes a lot of explicit definitions of these concepts, and also a lot of human discussion about them. But can these concepts emerge on their own, even without explicit training? Testing this on LLMs is not practical - it would be very hard to hide all hints of moral values from the training corpus. Instead, we can test a purely visual model that was only trained on images, with no labels at all. This is the case for Meta’s open model, DINOv2 (Oquab et al.

Attribution: LessWrong [public_ideas] https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/bpxEdN7CeEJvkJyq4/attack-graphs-for-ai-takeover

Lots of people have written up specific scenarios for how AI takeover might happen. But any one particular path is highly contingent, because all the branching points mean there's exponentially many ways this can play out. Cybersecurity manages this combinatorial explosion with an attack graph, where we list out the modular stepping stones that an attacker might use to reach its end goal, to draw out which subgoals enable which other subgoals. Similarly, a scheming AI's first move would likely be to launch an unmonitored deployment, while its end goal may be some sort of weapon that gives it decisive strategic advantage over the humans. There's a few paths it might take to get there, but its attack graph might look something like this: For example, if it's wildly superintelligent then it can probably just build crazy nanotech. Similarly if it's smart enough to run RSI while aligning its successor. Otherwise, its endgame probably doesn't involve any branch of science beyond the ken of humans, and so it's not futile to model what it has to do instead. Let's consider these.

TLDR: LLMs uplift novices in setting up wetlab equipment and can sort of move things around, but probably still need expert help There's a lot of talk recently about this chart and AI pretraining algorithmic progress going superexponential, but even the best algorithm needs training data to be useful. One of the most data scarce areas is biology, which makes sense because your RL environment verifier is a wetlab and rats instead of unit tests and the Lean 4 compiler. An interesting and IMO understudied aspect of RSI is AI increasing biological data generation, both from new assays and reducing the barrier to entry to wetlab work. Traditionally, everyone from startups to big pharma outsourced their wetlab work to Contract Research Organizations (CROs) such as IQVIA, WuXi AppTec, Pharmaron, Charles River, etc. You come up with a set of experiments you want to run, pay 6 to 7 figures, wait a few months for the reagents to ship and cells to grow and you get your data. Recently, everyone and their grandmother is going into biology.

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: LessWrong [public_ideas] https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/Foq3GrbvKoLGbfxdc/r-and-d-compute-explains-much-of-anthropic-s-acceleration

METR's report estimates that Anthropic's AI R&D has accelerated in the past year, and that 80% of this acceleration is due to AI itself. But if AI accelerated Anthropic researchers, Anthropic would have a strong incentive to scale up its R&D compute proportionally to AI uplift. Accounting for this scaleup reduces the AI-attributed share of acceleration to <50%, and favors AI regulations that restrict R&D compute. Experiments and labor Software progress comes from trying ideas and seeing which ones work. Researchers come up with the ideas and write the code to test them, and R&D compute runs the tests of these ideas. Each input is only as useful as the other allows: researchers without compute can't find out which of their ideas work, and compute without researchers has nothing worth running. We can represent this dynamic with a model where research labor (whether AI or human) is combined with R&D compute to generate software progress. One specific way to model this relationship is with Ryan Greenblatt’s model, in which software progress is proportional to (labor)^0.

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline

Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/books/history-of-paperback-books/

We live in a time of technological revolution. The past 50 years have birthed the personal computer, the smartphone, and now artificial intelligence. While each is a world-changing invention and still relatively young, none yet rivals the movable-type printing press. Starting around 1440 in Mainz, Germany, Johannes Gutenberg’s invention enabled information to spread as never before. It cultivated ideas, seeded revolutions, and so much more. It also gave birth to a new industry: bookselling. Though it’s hard to imagine today — with overstuffed bookshelves decorating any toddler’s bedroom and little free libraries as fixtures on city streets — books were almost exclusively sold to society’s elite for hundreds of years. “The range of available customers and books was much narrower than we are accustomed to today, partly because books were still expensive,” Andrew Pettegree, the Bishop Wardlaw Professor of History at the University of St. Andrews, writes in his recently published book, The Bookshop: A History of Bookselling from the Dawn of Print to the Twenty-First Century.

### Ask Ethan: What does it mean for atoms to “touch” each other?
Source: Big Think
Published: 2026-11-27 07:00 UTC
URL: https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-bang/do-atoms-touch/
Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-bang/do-atoms-touch/

One of the most counterintuitive things about existence is the notion of forces. In order to experience a force — that is, for one object to feel the influence of another object on it — two objects don’t necessarily even need to touch, or be in contact, with one another. Objects on Earth’s surface feel Earth’s gravity, but so do airplanes, satellites, and even the Moon: in the atmosphere, in low-Earth orbit, or even hundreds of thousands of kilometers away. An electrically charged object attracts and repels other electrical charges, regardless of how far away they are from each other. And, in a more familiar fashion, two magnets flipped so that their north poles face each other mutually repel one another so strongly that, for some magnets, even the strongest humans cannot bring them together into contact. So what happens, then, when you try to bring your thumb and forefinger together? How close do they actually get, and do they ever truly “touch” one another?

### How propagandists weaponize archaeology to rewrite the past
Source: Big Think
Published: 2026-11-26 15:30 UTC

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/history-society/how-propagandists-weaponize-archaeology/

The historian Eric Hobsbawm once said, “Historians are to nationalism what poppy-growers … are to heroin-addicts. [They] supply the essential raw material.” The same holds true for archaeologists. The heritage archaeologists reveal helps groups of people forge collective identities and anchor our fleeting lives in something enduring. Spectacular discoveries — King Tut’s mask, the bronzes of Benin, Irish harps — also become national icons and rallying points. Regrettably, people with political agendas know this and often treat the past as ready-made propaganda — a bin to root through for “evidence” that justifies their goals. And if they can’t find what they need, they have no compunctions about twisting archaeology to suit their purposes. Consider the Peking Man fossils from China. Despite the singular name, these fossils consist of 40-odd men, women, and children unearthed 30 miles from Beijing starting in 1929. They belong to a hominin subspecies called Homo erectus pekinensis and lived 410,000 to 780,000 years ago.

13.8 billion years ago, what we know today as our observable Universe began with the most important origin event in cosmic history: the hot Big Bang. Once the Universe became filled with matter, antimatter, and radiation in an almost-perfectly uniform fashion, it expanded and gravitated in nearly perfect balance. As the Universe cooled, the matter and antimatter annihilated away, leaving a tiny, minuscule, but significant amount of matter behind. After 9.2 billion years, what would become our Solar System gradually began to form from a collapsing cloud of molecular gas, and after another 4.55 billion years or so, humanity first arose on planet Earth. When we look out at the Universe from our perspective in the here-and-now, we only get a snapshot of all of existence: defined by the properties of the light, particles, and gravitational waves that we observe at the moment of their arrival.

Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/mini-philosophy/the-facts-you-learned-at-school-that-other-countries-tell-differently/

“There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them because it’s sort of obvious.” Last week, I spoke with Jimmy Wales — the man responsible for Wikipedia, the darling of students all over the world since 2001. Our conversation meandered pleasantly over philosophy, technology, cryptocurrency, politics, history, and more. (Big Think members can get first access to watch the full video at this link.) But Wales’s fish parable hit me. What “water” do I swim in? Of course, you can take this two ways. First, the water can be seen broadly: the slightly opaque “ways of thinking” we operate under in the 21st-century post-Enlightenment West. We’ll park that discussion for another day. But we can also see this “water” more practically: What specific facts or pieces of information do I think I know, but aren’t as “obvious” as I thought?

Attribution: MUBI Notebook [film_moving_image] https://mubi.com/en/notebook/posts/a-sharing-of-souls-ryusuke-hamaguchi-discusses-all-of-a-sudden

All of a Sudden (Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, 2026). At 197 minutes, Ryûsuke Hamaguchi’s latest film, All of a Sudden (2026), is neither the longest nor the most radical of the Japanese director’s dozen-plus features. In fact, its story, about two women of different cultural backgrounds who meet and grow close over the course of a few weeks, is decidedly straightforward and occasionally even sentimental—a far cry from the convoluted, miserabilist narratives that tend to dominate the world of international art cinema. Inspired by When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher with Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, a collection of epistolary nonfiction written by two Japanese intellectuals, All of a Sudden is deceptively complex despite its surface-level linearity; for a filmmaker synonymous with sprawling social mosaics (Happy Hour, 2015) and ambitious literary adaptations (Asako I & II, 2018; the Oscar-winning Drive My Car, 2021), it’s the 47-year-old Hamaguchi’s richest and most direct work to date.

Source: MUBI Notebook

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe

Attribution: MUBI Notebook [film_moving_image] https://mubi.com/en/notebook/posts/a-world-in-parts

The Journey (Peter Watkins, 1987). At Radio Canada, preparations are underway for Ronald Reagan’s 1985 summit with Canadian prime minister Brian Mulroney. Filmmaker Peter Watkins and his crew have been allowed into meetings where the broadcasters plan their coverage down to the second. Everyone must synchronize their watches: A discrepancy of 40 seconds, one participant warns, could throw off the day’s work. A shot requested at 17:02 might be missed if recorded 30 seconds later. “One thing is certain: there can’t be anything unexpected tonight,” another member of the team declares. Security officials will provide the presidential route, street by street, allowing the text to be prepared beforehand. “What you don’t have is the images.” Even the moment Reagan is scheduled to go behind the curtains to shake hands has been fixed: 9:03, already too late for the broadcasters’ purposes. Watkins’s voiceover draws our attention to the “constant emphasis on control and brevity.” What will later arrive in the viewer’s living room as news has, in one sense, already happened.

In this episode, the conversation explores Rodrigo Sorogoyen and Diego Luna’s earliest cinematic experiences and how trust and a sense of togetherness form the foundation of their approach to working with actors. Rodrigo Sorogoyen is a Spanish director and screenwriter whose work spans nearly twenty feature films, series and short films. His filmography moves between intricate narratives rooted in political and crime thrillers, and deeply intimate and socially driven dramas. His 2017 short film Madre was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film and later became the starting point for a 2019 feature-length adaptation, which premiered in the Orizzonti section of the Venice Film Festival. In 2022, he presented The Beasts at the Cannes Film Festival, earning the César Award for Best Foreign Film, Goya Awards for Best Director and Best Original Screenplay, and the San Sebastián Film Festival Audience Award. He also co-wrote and co-directed the romantic series The New Years (2024).

Trump. Abassi tells host Rico Gagliano about both, and what it was like to navigate two very different kinds of censorship. The MUBI Podcast returns for its 12th season, “Under Pressure.” At a time when artists worldwide are being threatened or stifled by their governments, host Rico Gagliano tells the stories of filmmakers from across history and around the world who have made movies in spite of incredible state pressure to compromise, give in, or give up. From 1970s Turkey to modern-day America, these are alternately wild, sobering, controversial, and inspiring tales of art by any means necessary. Listen to episode two below or wherever you get your podcasts: Apple Podcasts Spotify More

Attribution: MUBI Notebook [film_moving_image] https://mubi.com/en/notebook/posts/the-last-emperor-a-conversation-with-jeremy-thomas

The Last Emperor (Bernardo Bertolucci, 1987). When Jeremy Thomas died on September 11, 2026, the British film industry lost a titan. A producer who paid no heed to the vagaries of popular culture, Thomas was led by his impeccable palate for cinematic ambition, unswayed by whether audiences or critics came along for the ride. A list of filmmakers whose work makes up Thomas’s production portfolio reads like a who’s who of maverick visionaries, each of them fiercely loyal to the last: Nicolas Roeg and David Cronenberg; Takeshi Kitano and Jonathan Glazer; Nagisa Ōshima and Wim Wenders; Jerzy Skolimowski and Bernardo Bertolucci, whose The Last Emperor (1987) won Thomas the Academy Award for Best Picture. Cinema ran through Thomas’s veins. Both his father and uncle were filmmakers, respectively behind the uniquely British series of Doctor (1954–70) and Carry On (1958–92) films, and Thomas spent much of his youth on the sound stages at Pinewood Studios.

### “There was this idea in the 1800s of carillons being Romantic glitch machines”: Cory Arcangel
Source: The Wire Magazine
Published: 2026-11-25 00:00 UTC
URL: https://www.thewire.co.uk/in-writing/interviews/Cory-arcangel-interview-glitch-machines
Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Wire Magazine [music_sound] https://www.thewire.co.uk/in-writing/interviews/Cory-arcangel-interview-glitch-machines

Robert Barry speaks to Cory Arcangel about his new work for 12-bell carillon, as well as a new project that combines scores with knitting patterns “Carillons were one of the first music computers,” Cory Arcangel tells me. “They were played by these drums, like a music box – or like a MIDI computer, basically.” His new installation, X, on view now in the 17 hectare sculpture garden of Norway’s Kistefos Museum, is a 12-bell carillon housed in a mobile phone tower which randomly generates a unique dodecaphonic composition every hour, on the hour, before gradually removing the notes from the tone row, one by one. Installed this summer, it is the park’s first sound sculpture. And while it is built into one of the most visible artefacts of the modern telecommunications industry, it is also a reminder that bell towers have always been a kind of media. Born in Buffalo, New York, Arcangel first came to prominence in the early years of this century as part of a wave of visual artists fascinated by – and intent on subverting – the protocols and aesthetics of the world wide web.

In this extract, taken from “The Myth And Mystery Of The New Blockaders”, Nick Soulsby outlines the unique biographical challenges in documenting the lives of North East refuseniks Richard and Philip Rupenus It’s common in biography for the sense of the person to become overwhelmed by their actions: the politician fades beneath crises and legislation; the general into a catalogue of battlefield decisions; the musician into the cycle of writing, recording and performing. Once set in motion, most lives worth writing of become dominated by a body of work with the human being whittled away to a delivery mechanism for its creation: “…A man takes a job and that job becomes what he is…You do a thing and that’s what you are…You get a job, you become the job,” as a character in Taxi Driver explains to Travis Bickle. In the case of The New Blockaders (TNB), to have the work stand on its own account was not, initially, extraordinary: so many artists leave interpretation to their audiences or keep a gap between work and life.

To accompany his Unlimited Editions report in The Wire 514, Tim Fish compiles an annotated playlist of tracks from the Liverpool label When Blah Records emerged into the UK’s hiphop landscape in 2006, they formed part of an alternative movement to a rather dominant London scene. Co-founded by Lee Scott and Alex Jennings (aka Molotov), the label was primarily a way to officially distribute music for the rap crew Children Of The Damned (COTD), and the majority of artists who have put out records on the label over the subsequent 20 years have all had some real-life connection to Scott. The following playlist outlines some of Blah's most significant records. Children Of The Damned “Cold Sag Run Marathon” From Brick Pelican (2009) Children Of The Damned were the original Blah artists and they still remain at the core of the label today, albeit with expanded numbers and a slightly different name. This track gives a flavour of their origins and an even better indicator of how much their sound has evolved.

### Mark Korven: Borderline Sonics and Dimensional Demarcation
Source: The Wire Magazine
Published: 2026-11-16 00:00 UTC
URL: https://www.thewire.co.uk/in-writing/columns/mark-korven-borderline-sonics-and-dimensional-demarcation
Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Wire Magazine [music_sound] https://www.thewire.co.uk/in-writing/columns/mark-korven-borderline-sonics-and-dimensional-demarcation

Mark Korven’s scores for The Black Phone (2021) and Them (2021) destabilise hermetic soundworlds to convey psychological violence, writes Philip Brophy in his latest Secret History of Film Music column The contribution of Canadian composer Mark Korven to contemporary horror cinema is aligned with composers who sculpt their scores through tactile manipulation. His self-built Apprehension Engine, a hybrid guitar-percussion instrument, empowers distinctive acoustic control. Korven commissioned Toronto based guitar maker Tony Duggan-Smith to build the modest box incorporating tools and techniques favoured by Korven: a hurdy-gurdy for cranking, a spring reverb for metallic resonance, metal rods and wooden tongues for bowing (similar to the waterphone), and a stretched wire for E-bowing. Its abject sonics pepper Robert Eggers’s The Lighthouse (2019) with terse shudders and emotional spikes, and are also audible in Adam Schindler and Brian Netto’s Don’t Move (2024).

Source: ArchDaily

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe

Attribution: ArchDaily [architecture_urbanism] https://www.archdaily.com/1189051/borrowed-references-local-languages-blended-styles-on-latin-american-facades

Architectural styles are often identified through a familiar set of characteristics: particular forms, materials, proportions, and decorative elements. Yet these characteristics do not always remain tied to the traditions from which they originate. A classical column may appear on a self-built house, a modernist ceramic composition may be reproduced across a residential façade, or a chalet may become part of a multistory commercial building. Each retains something recognizable from its precedent, although its application reflects a different set of architectural decisions.

Located in a high-rise office building in Qianhai, Shenzhen, UDC is a multifunctional space that brings together fashion retail, work, social activities, and brand events. Through this project, we explored how to move beyond the fixed boundaries between different activities, allowing them to connect and overlap within the same space to create new spatial experiences.

In Ayllón (Segovia), adjacent to the historic center, the openings of a 1910 facade now look out onto a courtyard. The facade originally belonged to a family home that was divided into two dwellings in the mid-1940s. Decades later, the owner reunited one of those halves with two adjacent plots to build his primary residence. He wanted a house that could be navigated without steps, and where proximity to the street was compatible with family privacy.

In the grim darkness of the week before the release of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4, developers King Art and publishers Deep Silver have released a demo model painter. It's your chance to pre-emptively run a brush over units from the new strategy game's four major factions – Orks, Adeptus Mechanicus, Necrons and Space Marines. The Imperial Guard are in the game too, but mostly as a tutorial army. What a slap in the face for the Imperium's vanilla humans. Deep Silver are calling it "the most powerful Painter in Dawn of War history", which doesn't seem all that dashing a boast given that Dawn of War 3 came out almost 10 years ago and today's PCs have a fair bit more RAM in them. You can opt for Basic Painter mode in order to quickly knock together livery for entire armies, or fire up the Advanced Painter and get stuck into the weeds of individual armour and body parts, with a choice of materials, patterns, decals and weathering. Here be trailer. Read more

Glagstone's "1-bit" aesthetic is a homage to Macintosh games of the late 1980s, cut with elements of art deco, Expressionism and film noir, but it looks like that mainly because it began life on lo-fi indie handheld Playdate. In transplanting this eerie, story-driven city-builder to Steam, developers Valerii Krasnoselskii and Evgenii Kirichenko have fleshed out the tasty throwback art and shored up connections between the game's management and story layers, while leaving the crux of the experience untouched: you are the newly appointed governor of a remote northern island, contested by rival nations. You have come here to harvest the island's rich mineral resources, and now, the island is trying to drive you nuts. Read more

### Exposure matters more than persuasiveness for digital mass persuasion
Source: Nature Human Behaviour
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-026-02644-9
Source meta: journal · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:48 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Nature Human Behaviour [human_societies] https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-026-02644-9

Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02644-9 The persuasive impact of digital media content depends both on its persuasiveness per person and on how many people are exposed to it, and there is greater variability in exposure than persuasiveness across content. Together, these facts suggest exposure matters more than persuasiveness for digital mass persuasion.

We discuss how researchers, funders and journals can draw lasting value from urgency-driven research.

### ESG reporting perceptions from lecturer perspectives: The case of Vietnamese Universities
Source: PLOS ONE Biology
Published: 2026-11-25 14:00 UTC
URL: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0363891
Source meta: journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal
Updated: 2026-11-25 14:00 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:49 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: PLOS ONE Biology [academic_research] https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0363891

by Thi Phuong Dung Nguyen, Ha Dac Viet Nguyen, Ha Phuong Nguyen, Thi Thanh Hong Pham Higher education institutions play a key role in developing Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) expertise and knowledge. Lecturers are central to translating ESG strategies into educational and organizational outcomes, yet their perceptions of ESG reporting remain under-explored in Vietnam. This study examines individual and institutional factors associated with lecturers’ perceptions of ESG reporting, drawing on the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), Institutional Theory, Stakeholder Theory, and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory. Survey data from 437 eligible university lecturers in Vietnam were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Results show significant positive associations for innovation policies, sustainability action programs, social pressure, attitude, perceived usefulness, and knowledge, while subjective norm and leadership show no significant direct associations.

Preventing children's exposure to hardship, trauma, and abuse in childhood is a global public health priority. This exposure is associated with a substantial burden of disease and is one of the most important risk factors for experience and perpetration of violence against women, with all the entailed health consequences.1–3 Over recent years, research on and development of interventions to prevent child abuse and neglect through strengthening of parenting have intensified. Reviews show considerable success with some interventions, including in llow-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), but also signal room for further work developing scalable, affordable interventions.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with increasing global burden driven by population growth and ageing, persistent harmful exposures, and substantial health inequities. The Lancet Commission on COPD articulated an ambitious vision for disease elimination with prevention, early detection, and intervention. This Review revisits that vision, assesses progress since 2022, and calls for a broader commitment to lifelong lung health as an update of the Commission.

Cording is a century-old mycobacterial virulence trait. CryoET and light microscopy reveal that incomplete cell separation during division generates a shared interbacterial membrane. The planet Mercury might be one of the least explored planetary bodies in the solar system, but its is arguably the most crucial in helping scientists better understand the formation and evolution of the inner solar system. Its position as the closest planet to the Sun makes it a prime target for how the rocky planets formed and evolved and what this could mean for finding life beyond Earth. However, just traveling to Mercury is a lengthy and time-consuming effort, often taking a spacecraft several years just to achieve orbit. More on that later.

The last few days we’ve been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently – maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution? According to another paper from Dr. Turyshev, released as a preprint on arXiv, it all depends on the mission requirements.

Attribution: Phys.org Mollusks [mollusks] https://phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-sea-mollusk-houses-bacteria.html

Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.

This post From New Variant to New Species: Unraveling the Mystery of the Pasture Mealybug appeared first on Entomology Today - Brought to you by the Entomological Society of America. A tiny, wax-covered scale insect found damaging pasture grasses and sugarcane in North America and Australia has been challenging to simply identify. When the bug arrived in Florida earlier this year, taxonomists at the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, working with the United States Department of Agriculture, acted quickly to analyze the insect's morphology and genetics, discovering that the pestiferous pasture mealybug spreading throughout the New World represents a new species, Heliococcus novovillei. It's a key first step in knowing how to respond to manage the new invasive pest. AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line. "Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: https://www.theregister.com/networks/2026/11/24/fcc-proposes-tit-for-tat-restrictions-on-foreign-satellite-operators/5311889 The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote in December on proposals [PDF] that would restrict foreign satellite operators in the same way their home countries restrict US providers. The telecoms regulator says the move is to "ensure reciprocity and fair dealing" in the rules governing satellite operators. The main aim appears to be hitting back at European efforts to build up the region's own space communications industries. According to the FCC, the US has so far welcomed satellite systems licensed abroad on a level playing field, but that regulators elsewhere have begun holding US systems to different rules than they apply to their own domestic suppliers. "This has operated to the disadvantage of American satellite providers that are or may be burdened with regulatory and spectrum limitations that their competitors in foreign nations simply do not face," said FCC chairman Brendan Carr.

### AI Comes Up With Bizarre Physics Experiments. But They Work.
Source: SoylentNews
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://soylentnews.org/article.pl?sid=26/11/26/1833218&from=rss
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: SoylentNews [computing_cultures] https://soylentnews.org/article.pl?sid=26/11/26/1833218&from=rss

Snotnose writes: I recently read a story like this only with computer designs. There are precision measurements, and then there's the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory. In each of LIGO's twin gravitational wave detectors (one in Hanford, Washington, and the other in Livingston, Louisiana), laser beams bounce back and forth down the four-kilometer arms of a giant L. When a gravitational wave passes through, the length of one arm changes relative to the other by less than the width of a proton. It's by measuring these minuscule differences — a sensitivity akin to sensing the distance to the star Alpha Centauri down to the width of a human hair — that discoveries are made. Rana Adhikari, a physicist at the California Institute of Technology, led the detector optimization team in the mid-2000s. He and a handful of collaborators painstakingly honed parts of the LIGO design, exploring the contours of every limit that stood in the way of a more sensitive machine.

It was a background utility that just worked. However, datacenters are no longer passive consumers of electricity. They are becoming active participants in energy generation, storage, and grid management through behind-the-meter infrastructure. This is being driven by the explosive rise of AI and a manufacturing renaissance. Power demand is growing again, increasing an average of 2.1 percent annually over the past five years, with datacenters emerging as a dominant driver of long-term growth. Electric Power Research Institute projects that datacenters could consume as much as 17 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030, more than triple their current 4-5 percent share. This massive spike in demand is clashing directly with a severely constrained power grid.

### sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
Source: Simon Willison's Weblog
Published: 2026-11-26 06:08 UTC
URL: https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/26/sqlite3-rsync/
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Updated: 2026-11-26 06:08 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:49 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Simon Willison's Weblog [computing_cultures] https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/26/sqlite3-rsync/

sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025. It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO. In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side.

Early in the 7.4 merge window, Greg Kroah-Hartman applied a patch that caused the kernel to be marked as tainted whenever user space manually binds or unbinds a device driver to a device. This change was meant to be a defense against a flood of spurious bug reports generated by fuzzers, but it also turned out to get in the way of some real use cases. After some discussion, the patch has been reverted, but this situation hints at an area where better kernel interfaces are needed.

Marcus Borg recounts an experiment to investigate if healthy code was cheaper for agents to review. Between a typical unhealthy pull request (CodeHealth 2.8) and a typical healthy one (9.7), that adds up to 22 to 35%. The measures of health come from CodeScene. The experiment looked at three LLMs, 465 pull requests on 246 open source repositories. Each pull request was put through a review and fix pipeline involving five agents. They also looked at which code smells led to increased costs: they highlighted Complex Method and Complex Conditional from the smells identified by CodeScene. Another drop of evidence that good quality code matters in agentic engineering. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Gergely Orosz: One usage for AI: for these 100-page-long terms-and-service agreements you NEED to agree to, to eg play the game / sign up for a $10/month service and can never ever ever read as a regular person: I paste into AI and ask: “anything weird in this?” Before hitting “agree” ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Andrew Sharp has a good analysis of Jensen Huang and the crisis at Nvidia.

Data contracts are a way to describe the contents and guarantees of datasets. Simon Harrer and Arif Wider describe in detail what they are and how to use them. They apply practices from API design to data by treating them as data-providing services - such as data products - whose interfaces we want to define as clearly as possible. This approach significantly increases the robustness of large-scale data landscapes, and gives both people and AI agents the explicit, trustworthy metadata they need to work with data autonomously, which is why more and more enterprises are adopting them. more…

Distributed systems are hard to test because partial failures overlap with live traffic and the same fault can produce different execution traces on different runs. Unmesh Joshi describes how deterministic simulation testing addresses this by replacing real clocks, networks, and storage with simulated components driven by a single-threaded execution loop. This allows simulating both hard failures and routine slowdowns—such as network and disk latency spikes—and more importantly makes every execution reproducible. This article explains the technique using a quorum key-value store as a running example, with code from Tickloom, a Java implementation of the approach. more…

### Bliki: Generated Glossary
Source: Martin Fowler
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GeneratedGlossary.html
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R5 · P5 · baseline
Updated: 2026-11-12 14:15 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:49 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GeneratedGlossary.html

When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job. The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion.

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/articles/tests-as-data.html

Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors. Matteo Vaccari makes three claims: (1) when AI writes the code, developers become its customers; (2) therefore customer tests, not developer tests, become the primary contract between humans and AI; (3) moving that contract into test data rather than test code makes it easier to protect it from unexpected modifications by coding agents. All of this optimizes for human-readable tests that establish a contract between humans and AI. While in the past DSL parsers and custom test runners were expensive to write and maintain, now AI makes them cheap. more…

It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends. One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands?

Hello! I’ve been working on a Django site recently, and I decided to use SQLite as the database. When I was getting started with using SQLite as database for a website I read a bunch of blog posts about how it is totally fine to use SQLite in production for a small site and I think it is totally fine, but what I did not fully appreciate is that SQLite is still a database, databases are complicated, and I do not know a lot about operating databases. So here are a couple of small things I’ve been learning about running SQLite. This is the 4th website I’ve used SQLite for, and I think this one is harder because with the power of the Django ORM I’ve been making the database do more work than I was previously without Django. I started by turning on WAL mode like all the blog posts said to do and hoping for the best. ANALYZE is apparently important Today I was running a query (using SQLite’s FTS5 for full-text search) on a table with 4000 rows and it took 5 seconds. That seemed wrong to me: computers are fast! It turned out that what I needed to do was to run ANALYZE!

Hello! One of my long term projects on here is figuring out how to write frontend Javascript without using Node or any other server JS runtime. One issue I run into a lot in my frontend JS projects is that I don’t know how to write tests for them. I’ve tried to use Playwright in the past, but it felt slow and unwieldy to be starting these new browser processes all the time, and it involved some Node code to orchestrate the tests. The result is that I just don’t test my frontend code which doesn’t feel great. Usually I don’t update my projects much either so it doesn’t come up that much, but it would be nice to be able to make changes with more confidence! So a way to do frontend testing that I like has been on my wishlist for a long time. idea: just run the tests in the browser tab Alex Chan wrote a great post a while back called Testing JavaScript without a (third-party) framework in response to one of my previous posts in this series that explained how to write a tiny unit-testing framework that runs in a page in browser.

Workflow SDK 5.8 runs workflows on a new execution engine, rebuilt for performance. Step-to-step latency is 12x lower, and large fan-outs, like running 256 steps in parallel, use 14x less function time outside your step code. This directly improves turn times for durable AI agents, among many other improvements. To get the new engine, upgrade to workflow@5.8.0 or later. New runs will use the new engine by default, and runs already started on an older version will safely keep running on that version. Make sure your steps are idempotent where possible to get the most out of this upgrade. Drastically reduced overhead In our benchmarks comparing 5.2.0 to 5.8.0, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 85 ms to 7 ms. The median run, including 102 seconds of step work, finished in 111 seconds instead of 3.0 minutes. Running 256 parallel steps in a fan-out added 5.5× less overhead, 2.5 seconds instead of 13.5 seconds, and the median run spent 14× less time in functions beyond the steps' own work, 105 seconds instead of 1,446.

Legacy runtimes, such as node22, now use the open-source images in the vercel/sandbox repository, distributed through Vercel Container Registry (VCR). That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough.

Enterprise teams using Secure Compute can now create and manage AWS PrivateLink endpoints directly from the Vercel dashboard. Endpoints on Secure Compute live in your team's dedicated VPC and use the network's AWS region. They belong to the network and are shared by its connected project environments. Vercel Functions, Vercel Sandbox, and builds connected to the network can reach AWS-hosted backends over the AWS private network. Before you add an endpoint in Vercel, the backend must already be exposed through a published AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. Examples include RDS, Aurora, Redshift, Snowflake, MongoDB Atlas, and internal services behind a Network Load Balancer. In Team Settings → Networking, open your Secure Compute network and choose Add Endpoint from the PrivateLink tab. Standard pricing for new endpoints: Each Secure Compute network includes one AWS PrivateLink endpoint. Additional endpoints cost $30 per month each. PrivateLink data transfer costs $0.04 per GB. With flags@4.5.0, projects on Vercel can use Flags Explorer and precompute without FLAGS_SECRET. That cuts out a setup step for new projects and removes the need to keep a shared secret in sync across microfrontends. Vercel signs Flags Explorer discovery requests and overrides, and the SDK encrypts flag values shown in the Vercel Toolbar with Vercel’s public key. Existing projects keep using FLAGS_SECRET while the environment variable is set or the secret is passed in code. Upgrading alone doesn't switch them to Vercel-managed keys. To use Vercel-managed keys for these features, remove the environment variable and any code that passes the secret explicitly. For local development, run vercel env pull. Precomputed codes created without a secret work only in the deployment that created them. Precompute without a secret requires Vercel system environment variables, which are enabled by default. Prebuilt deployments and codes that must work across deployments still need a secret; use FLAGS_PRECOMPUTE_SECRET if only precompute needs one.

Deprecations and removals for Kubernetes v1.38 kubectl: WebSocket opt-out environment variables removed kubectl has used WebSockets instead of SPDY by default for kubectl exec, attach and cp since v1.30, and for kubectl port-forward since v1.31. Attribution: Google Cloud Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/how-to-fix-your-teams-api-keys/

Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down. The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config. For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage company, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see. Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? ### Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
Source: Kubernetes Blog
Published: 2026-11-16 18:35 UTC
URL: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/11/16/ipvs-removal/
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-28 13:49 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Kubernetes Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/11/16/ipvs-removal/

The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly. In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40.
